title: Navigating a Four-Day Week and an Employment Tribunal with Long COVID
transcript:
[00:00:05] INT: Okay, the recorder is going. Thank you so much for making time for this today, Gareth. Just to confirm for the tape, I'm Sarah from the University of Wessex, and we're doing the Working with Long COVID study. You've already signed the consent form, and you know you can pause or stop whenever you need to, especially if fatigue kicks in.
[00:00:24] P: Yeah, thanks Sarah. Honestly, I'm alright at the moment, I had a decent-ish morning, which is rare enough. And I've got my water here. So yeah, fire away.
[00:00:34] INT: Brilliant. Could we start with a bit of background? Just tell me about yourself, what you do for work, and when you first got ill.
[00:00:43] P: Sure. So, I'm Gareth Pritchard, I'm thirty-nine, live in Basingham with my wife Claire and our two kids—Theo, he's seven, and Maya, she's four. I've been a civil servant for nearly twelve years now. I work for the Department for Civic Infrastructure, in the Maritime Licensing and Coastal Policy Team. It's quite niche, actually—my main patch before all this was drafting statutory instruments for historic lighthouse decommissions, which sounds dead dry, I know, but I genuinely loved it. Proper nerdy detail.
[00:01:21] INT: That does sound very specific! And when did COVID first hit you?
[00:01:26] P: It was the 14th of March 2022. I remember because it was the week before Maya's second birthday. Just a bog-standard positive lateral flow, felt rough for ten days, and I thought, right, I'll bounce back. Except I didn't. By May, I was still waking up feeling like I'd been hit by a lorry. The brain fog was terrifying—I'd open a policy brief and the words would just swim. I went to my GP at Oakfield Medical Practice, Dr. Sunita Rao, and she was actually really good, to be fair. She didn't fob me off with anxiety. She referred me to the Long COVID Clinic at St Jude's General Hospital, though the wait was about seven months.
[00:02:14] INT: Seven months is a long time to be in limbo. How were you managing work during that stretch?
[00:02:21] P: Badly. Really badly. I was off sick from April right through to the 3rd of October 2022. When I tried to do a phased return, my line manager at the time—Sandra Kettle—she was polite on the surface, you know, all "take care of yourself, Gareth," but the workload didn't actually shrink. I'd log on for four hours and find twenty-five urgent emails waiting. And because of the post-exertional malaise, if I pushed through a Tuesday, I'd be flat on my back in a dark room on Wednesday and Thursday. My heart rate would shoot up just walking up the stairs at home. Eventually St Jude's diagnosed me with Long COVID and secondary PoTS—Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome.
[00:03:12] INT: Right, so you had a formal diagnosis. Did that change how you talked to your employer about it?
[00:03:19] P: I thought it would. I disclosed everything to Sandra and HR. I even sent them the clinic letter—well, a redacted bit, though I think my NHS number 999 482 7103 was still on the top corner because I was too foggy to notice. I asked for a referral to Occupational Health. I saw Dr. Alistair Finch in January 2023, and his report was crystal clear: I was likely covered under the Equality Act, I needed reduced hours, home working, and no early-morning meetings because my mornings are brutal.
[00:03:56] INT: And how did Sandra respond to that report?
[00:04:01] P: She dragged her feet for months. Kept saying the Maritime Licensing and Coastal Policy Team needed "operational presence" in the Basingham office two days a week. Even though half the team dials in from other hubs anyway! My colleague Dev Patel—who's been an absolute saint, honestly, covering for me when I've had migraines—he works from home four days a week just because of childcare, no fuss at all. But for me, suddenly it was a "business need." It felt personal.
[00:04:34] INT: That sounds exhausting to fight while you're already unwell. You mentioned you moved to a four-day week—how did that come about?
[00:04:43] P: Yeah, so on the 19th of June 2023, I formally moved to a four-day week, compressed? No, not compressed—reduced hours, so 0.8 FTE. I couldn't handle compressed hours, ten-hour days would have finished me off. Wednesdays off to recover. I had to take the pay cut, obviously. My full-time salary was £44,200, and dropping to four days took me down to £35,360. That's a massive chunk when you've got a £1,350 a month mortgage on our place on Meadowsweet Lane—we're at 14 Meadowsweet Lane, up in Larkhill—and nursery fees for Maya.
[00:05:27] INT: How has that financial drop affected you and Claire?
[00:05:32] P: Oh, it's been brutal. Claire's had to pick up extra shifts, and I feel this awful guilt, like I'm not pulling my weight. I did apply for Personal Independence Payment, PIP, and after a horrific assessment I was awarded standard daily living, which is about £290 a month. It helps, it pays for my prescriptions and the heating when I'm freezing cold from the PoTS, but it doesn't touch the sides of what I lost. And I'm on a whole pharmacy now—ivabradine for the heart rate, propranolol, sumatriptan when the migraines hit, and I'm paying privately for low-dose naltrexone because the NHS won't prescribe it. That's another forty quid a month.
[00:06:21] INT: You mentioned earlier that you're in an employment tribunal dispute now. Can you walk me through how it escalated to that?
[00:06:30] P: Yeah, sorry, I get a bit wound up talking about this, let me just take a sip of water. So, even after I dropped to four days, Sandra put me on an informal attendance management review because I'd had three separate migraine days in two months. Despite Dr. Alistair Finch's report saying disability-related absences should be discounted! Then in October, they refused my request to stay fully remote during winter—I'd asked to avoid the commute into town because the bus journey alone wipes me out. I put in a formal grievance on the 28th of November 2023. My union rep, Brenda Hargreaves from the Civil and Public Sector Union, she came with me to the hearing. They rejected the grievance out of hand. Said I was "not meeting the core attendance expectations of the grade."
[00:07:28] INT: God, that must have been a shock.
[00:07:31] P: It broke something in me, Sarah. I'd given the Department for Civic Infrastructure twelve years. My employee ID is DCI-88412—I've been there so long my number's five digits! And suddenly I'm a problem to be managed out. So Brenda helped me go through ACAS, early conciliation went nowhere, and I submitted my tribunal claim on the 12th of February 2024. Failure to make reasonable adjustments and discrimination arising from disability. The case number is ET/2409182/2024. We've got a preliminary hearing set for the 16th of September 2024.
[00:08:13] INT: How are you coping with the cognitive load of a tribunal alongside Long COVID?
[00:08:20] P: Honestly? I'm barely coping. Preparing the witness statement took me three weeks because I can only concentrate for about forty minutes before the brain fog slams down like a shutter. I had to set up a separate email just to keep the legal stuff straight from work—gareth.pritchard85@example.com—and I've got Brenda's number and the solicitor's number on speed dial. Actually, sorry, if you ever need to send me the transcript to check, use that email, or my mobile is 07700 900418, just text me first because I don't answer unknown numbers when I'm crashing.
[00:08:57] INT: I've got that, thank you, Gareth. We'll make sure to anonymise all of that in the transcript. Can I ask—how has all of this affected your sense of who you are, outside of being a civil servant and a claimant?
[00:09:11] P: [sighs] That's the hardest bit, really. Before March 2022, I was the guy who could do everything. I used to spend my weekends in the shed restoring Victorian brass barometers—proper fiddly, precision work, polishing gears, calibrating mercury tubes. I haven't touched a barometer in two years. My hands shake too much from the fatigue, and I can't stand at the workbench for more than ten minutes without feeling faint. It's like the old Gareth died and left this knackered ghost behind.
[00:09:48] INT: And what about at home, with Claire and the kids?
[00:09:53] P: Claire's amazing, she really is, but I can see she's burnt out too. She's basically a single parent half the week. Theo's old enough now to notice—the other day he asked why Daddy always has to lie on the sofa with an ice pack on his head. That wrecked me. I had a proper cry in the bathroom after he went to bed. You try to be present, you know? I read Maya her stories in bed because I can do that lying down. But I miss kicking a football in the park with Theo. I miss being reliable.
[00:10:31] INT: It sounds like you're carrying an enormous amount—the physical symptoms, the financial pressure, the tribunal, and the grief for your old life. What's keeping you going at the moment?
[00:10:44] P: Spite, partly! [laughs] No, seriously, I don't want Sandra Kettle and HR to win. If they can push me out after twelve years, what chance does someone on a fixed-term contract have? Brenda says we've got a strong case, and Dev's actually offered to give a witness statement about the remote-working double standard, which was brave of him. And honestly, the low-dose naltrexone has taken the edge off the chronic fatigue—maybe ten percent better, which doesn't sound like much, but ten percent means I can sit at the dinner table with my family most nights. I'm holding onto that.
[00:11:26] INT: That ten percent sounds huge. Is there anything else you'd like to add that we haven't covered?
[00:11:33] P: Just that people think Long COVID is being a bit tired. It's not. It's a full-time job just managing the symptoms, and then you have to fight your employer for basic dignity on top of it. I just hope the tribunal makes them listen.
[00:11:49] INT: Thank you so much for being so open with me, Gareth. I'm going to stop the recording now.
